structured_output.summary: The hypothesis tree is still empty, so I'm proposing hypotheses rather than citing existing ids. The most useful find is a public recipe for this same benchmark (Daniel-T-S-Adams/CIFAR-100-speedrun, the same build/prepare/train contract). A hackathon team (abdullah-athar/iterate-futurebiohackers, PR #3) adapted Keller Jordan's airbench and reports 75.29% mean accuracy in 8.11 s over 40 trials on an A100-SXM4-80GB, against the organizer's ResNet9-style baseline of 75.36% in 59.30 s (40 epochs). Their reported settings are: three convolutions per group with widths 128/384/576, plain Nesterov SGD with lr 9.0 and wd 0.012, label smoothing 0.3, 8.5 epochs, and no TTA. torch.compile and warmup run in the untimed build; GPU transfer, normalization and whitening init run in the timed prepare. They swept about 40 configs, and Muon lost to SGD at every model size. I could only read this through search-engine snippets because GitHub returned 404 when I tried to fetch the PR, so the exact code isn't verified. The airbench paper and code provide the rest of the toolkit: frozen patch-whitening first layer, Dirac init, a 64x LR boost on BN biases, Lookahead/EMA, alternating flip (about 27% effective speedup), a triangular LR schedule, channels_last with fp16, and max-autotune compile. Multi-crop TTA, which airbench relies on, is banned here. So any airbench-derived recipe loses that gain and needs a bit more training or capacity to make up for it. airbench96 with no tuning reaches 79.27% on CIFAR-100, which shows there is headroom above 75% to trade for time. Directions the tree hasn't covered yet: lower-resolution or progressive-resize early epochs, the Muon variant at different widths (it beat SGD on CIFAR-10 but lost on this CIFAR-100 recipe), dropping easy examples, and reducing overhead in prepare (whitening init on a small subset, a GPU-resident loader). One momentum-schedule paper reports faster early progress on CIFAR-100 but a 1.7-point final accuracy loss, which counts against that approach. Prior times were measured on SXM (400 W); the official judging GPU is PCIe (300 W) and will likely be somewhat slower.

findings.source: https://github.com/abdullah-athar/iterate-futurebiohackers/pull/3 (PR title + search snippets; page itself returned 404 on fetch)
findings.claim: Recipe for the same CIFAR-100 speedrun benchmark got 75.29% mean accuracy in 8.11 s (sd 0.02 s) over 40 trials on a Modal A100-SXM4-80GB. The organizer baseline is 75.36% in 59.30 s. The recipe was adapted from airbench: torch.compile and synthetic-data warmup in the untimed build(); GPU transfer, normalization and whitening init in the timed prepare(). The 8.5-epoch, last-width-576 config reached 75.5% in 8.11 s in their sweep.
findings.relevance: This is the nearest prior art and gives a starting point of about 8 s that meets the target. The accuracy margin is thin (75.29% mean over 40 seeds, just above 75%), and our 3-seed check requires >=0.753, so we may need slightly more epochs or width than they used.
hypotheses: Proposed H1: an airbench-style net (whitening + Dirac init + GPU-resident data + compile done in build) gets to 75% in about 8 s, far below the 59 s ResNet9 baseline
Proposed H1.1: time is dominated by epochs × width; their 8.5-epoch / 128-384-576 point is close to the Pareto frontier

findings.claim: Default hyperparameters: three convolutions per ConvGroup with widths 128/384/576, label smoothing 0.3, lr 9.0, wd 0.012, 8.5 epochs, chosen from about 40 configs swept on A100s. Muon lost to SGD at every model size and was removed. No TTA.
findings.relevance: These are concrete values to start from. Label smoothing 0.3 is higher than airbench's CIFAR-10 value of 0.2, which suggests stronger regularization helps with 100 classes. The Muon result argues against spending effort on Muon early.
hypotheses: Proposed H2: Nesterov SGD with airbench tricks beats Muon on CIFAR-100 under this time budget
Proposed H3.1: label smoothing around 0.3 beats 0.2 on CIFAR-100 at short schedules

findings.claim: Benchmark baseline: ResNet9-style, width 64, 40 epochs, 75.36% mean (trials 75.56% and 75.16%), mean prepare+train time 59.30 s, inference 0.117 s average (0.132 s max). Official judging uses an A100 80GB PCIe and 40 fresh trials.
findings.relevance: This gives the template's starting point. Even a straightforward port of airbench should cut time by roughly 7x.

findings.claim: airbench94: 2x2 whitening conv (24 channels, frozen weights from patch-covariance eigenvectors; biases trained for 3 epochs then frozen), Dirac init on later convs, widths 64/256/256, GELU, BN without affine weights, output scaled by 1/9. Nesterov SGD with batch 1024, lr 11.5, momentum 0.85, wd 0.0153, 64x LR on BN biases, label smoothing 0.2. Triangular LR schedule starting at 0.2x and peaking at 20% of training. Lookahead with alpha = 0.95^5 * (t/T)^3 every 5 steps. Alternating flip plus 2-px reflect translate. 9.9 epochs.
findings.relevance: This is the full set of tricks the 8 s CIFAR-100 recipe is built on. Each one is a candidate to tune or ablate.
hypotheses: Proposed H1.2: whitening + Dirac init + bias scaler + Lookahead each cut the epochs needed to reach target

findings.claim: Removing a component adds this many epochs to reach 94% on CIFAR-10: identity init about +2.9, scale-bias trick about +5.4, Lookahead about +1.5, multi-crop TTA about +1.1 (another version of the summary says TTA effect is minimal). Alternating flip instead of random flip gives a 27.1% effective speedup at 20 epochs without TTA.
findings.relevance: TTA is banned here, so airbench's TTA gain (roughly 1 epoch' worth) is lost and a CIFAR-10-tuned epoch count will fall short. Alternating flip is a free win.
hypotheses: Proposed H1.3: with TTA banned, about 1 more epoch (or equivalent width) is needed compared with an airbench recipe that uses TTA
Proposed H1.4: alternating flip cuts epochs-to-target by about 20–27% compared with random flip on CIFAR-100

findings.claim: Untuned airbench96 reaches 79.27% on CIFAR-100 without Cutout (79.76% with Cutout), compared with 77.54% and 78.04% for ResNet-18.
findings.relevance: There is about 4 points of headroom above 75%. The question is how cheaply it can be traded for time (fewer epochs, narrower nets). Cutout adds about 0.5 points at long schedules but may hurt at about 8 epochs.
hypotheses: Proposed H3: at short schedules, extra regularization (Cutout) costs more accuracy than it gains

findings.claim: airbench95 hyperparameters: widths 128/384/384, 15 epochs, batch 1024, lr 10.0, momentum 0.85, wd 0.0153, bias_scaler 64, label smoothing 0.2, whiten_bias_epochs 3, BN momentum 0.6, scaling 1/9, translate 2, TTA level 2.
findings.relevance: The CIFAR-100 recipe (128/384/576, three convs per group) sits between airbench95 and airbench96. Width is the main lever for accuracy per second.

findings.claim: airbench94_muon (2.59 s vs 3.09 s compiled SGD on CIFAR-10): Muon on 4D conv weights (lr 0.24, momentum 0.6, Nesterov, 3 Newton-Schulz steps), SGD for biases and head (lr 0.053 and 0.67, momentum 0.85). Batch 2000, 8 epochs, max-autotune torch.compile, channels_last, fp16 except BN in fp32, whitening from 5000 sampled images.
findings.relevance: On CIFAR-10, Muon plus batch 2000 was about 16% faster than SGD. The CIFAR-100 team found Muon worse, but they may not have tuned batch size or Muon lr. Settings worth borrowing regardless: max-autotune, channels_last, and whitening estimated from a 5000-image subset (cheaper prepare).
hypotheses: Proposed H2.1: Muon with retuned lr and batch 2000 could still beat SGD on CIFAR-100 (counter to the PR's finding)
Proposed H4: prepare overhead (whitening init, GPU transfer) is a measurable fraction of an ~8 s score and can be cut by using subset covariance

findings.claim: A critical-damping momentum schedule mu(t) = 1 - 2*sqrt(alpha(t)) reaches 90% on CIFAR-10 2.34x faster but ends 0.46 pp lower. On CIFAR-100 it gives 2–4x faster early progress but costs 1.7 pp final accuracy (5 seeds).
findings.relevance: This is evidence against momentum scheduling as a way to cut time: we are judged on final accuracy, and a 1.7 pp loss would wipe out the margin.
hypotheses: Proposed H2.2 (likely refuted a priori): a momentum schedule speeds up reaching 75%

findings.claim: Progressive resizing (small images early, full size late) speeds up training with negligible accuracy loss on ImageNet ResNets. For CIFAR, crop mode works better than resize. EfficientNetV2 pairs a smaller size with weaker regularization early on.
findings.relevance: Nobody has tried this on the airbench/CIFAR-100 speedrun yet. Early epochs at 24–28 px could cut FLOPs, though compile recompiling for a new shape (handle it in build) and BN statistics are risks.
hypotheses: Proposed H5: training the first ~half of epochs at reduced resolution lowers time at equal accuracy

findings.claim: airbench96_faster reaches 96% in 27.3 s (vs 34.7 s for airbench96) partly by filtering training data. On CIFAR-10, Muon took airbench94 from 3.09 s to 2.59 s.
findings.relevance: Skipping easy examples (or later-epoch subsampling) is another direction nobody has tried, but any proxy model must be trained inside the timed window. At about 8 s that probably isn't worth it unless the selection is nearly free (e.g., loss-based skipping during training).
hypotheses: Proposed H6: dropping low-loss examples in later epochs lowers time at equal accuracy
